sn56.11:1.1: This is the Buddha’s first discourse proper. In the narrative following the Buddha’s awakening (Kd 1:6.16.9), it follows the apparently fruitless encounter with Upaka on the road from Bodhgaya to Varanasi (MN 26:25.1), and precedes the teaching on not-self (SN 22.59). It is included in full in the later treatise the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Ps 2.6:1.1), and is alluded to many times in the Suttas, sometimes by name (MN 141:32.1), sometimes implicitly (MN 26:29.1). It is still a key text in Theravāda Buddhism, and is regularly memorized and recited.
sn56.11:1.2: These are the ascetics with whom the Bodhisatta practiced before rejecting their path of extreme asceticism (MN 36:20.2). The Buddha has traveled especially to teach them out of gratitude, because they were very helpful to him (MN 26:24.5). Their names are listed in the Vinaya account: Koṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji (Kd 1:6.31.6). | Note that he calls them “mendicants”, a term typically reserved for Buddhist renunciates. For a similar usage, see MN 140:3.4. In the Vinaya account, they ordained after this teaching.
sn56.11:2.3: The Buddha begins by finding common ground with the ascetics—the rejection of sensual pleasures, repudiating their idea that he had given himself up to luxury (see DN 29:23.2). Only then does he reject the five ascetics’ own practice of self-mortification. The descriptions in the Suttas make it clear that these practices were closely allied to the Jains, although the Buddha does not formally identify them (MN 85:10.2).
sn56.11:4.4: This definition clarifies two common misunderstandings. First, not all desire causes suffering, for some kinds of desire lead out of suffering (SN 51.15:4.1). Second, rebirth is not a tangential part of the Buddha’s teachings, uncritically inherited from cultural suppositions; it is baked into the fundamental meaning of the four noble truths. | The idiom tatratatra (literally “there, there”) is not selective (“here and there”) but distributive (“each and every place”, “everywhere”). By taking pleasure in sense experience, the mind binds itself to the need for continued stimulation in future lives. The distancing sense “there” is important, for craving does not merely satisfy itself with what it currently experiences, but must always seek out renewed gratification. For an Upaniṣadic precursor, see the note to the same idiom at MN 2:8.8.
sn56.11:4.5: Craving for sensual pleasures in this life or the next, binding oneself to a form that can experience such pleasures. In Buddhism, this includes not only the human realm, but all of the heavenly realms too, so far as the Brahmā realm. When a person has good kamma, they are reborn in a realm where they enjoy such pleasures, if not, in a lower realm. | Craving to continue existence (bhavataṇhā) refers to any desire, whether conscious or not, to continue existence after death. When it solidifies as a view it is called eternalism, and motivates religious and spiritual practices aiming at “eternal life”. As such, it especially applies to rebirth in the Brahmā realms. However, it is still present even in those who do not ascribe to such a view; craving is more primal than view (see SN 12.2:6.3 and notes). | Craving for nonexistence is the longing to destroy the self, in contrast with the Buddhist perspective that the self is a false construct. When it crystallizes as a view it is called annihilationism.
sn56.11:4.7: These are all terms for Nibbāna.
sn56.11:4.10: Thus the four noble truths include the noble eightfold path as the final factor, just as the path includes the truths as its first factor, right view. They are different perspectives on the same thing.
sn56.11:5.1: Each of the truths is analyzed in three “rounds”: the knowledge of each truth (saccañāṇa); the knowledge of what is to be done in respect to each truth (kiccañāṇa); and the completion of work (katañāṇa). Normally the realization of the four truths indicates stream-entry, which, if that applies here, suggests that the Buddha first attained stream-entry, then practiced according to the relevant duties, before culminating in arahantship. This progression through the stages of awakening could have happened in a single night.
sn56.11:5.2: Suffering should not be avoided, but should be “known all around”, “completely understood” (pariññeyyaṁ).
sn56.11:6.2: Note that it is not suffering that should be given up, but its cause.
sn56.11:7.2: “Should be realized” (sacchikātabbaṁ) is literally “should be seen with one’s own eyes”, “should be witnessed”.
sn56.11:8.2: “Developed” is literally “made to be more”, “amplified”, rather than brought into being from nothing. This implies that the potential is already present.
sn56.11:8.3: The Buddha rejects the idea that his fundamental insight was passed down through oral tradition. He had studied the texts of the Brahmins (MN 26:15.7) and showed a detailed knowledge of them, as I have documented extensively in my notes. He also shows knowledge of Jain texts, but does not actually say that he memorized them. He was not shy to adopt things he thought worthwhile, but he always insisted that the key teachings were discovered through his own experience.
sn56.11:9.1: The related passage at AN 8.64:10.1 shows that the “three rounds and twelve aspects” apply to the knowledge and vision, not the truths.
sn56.11:10.3: Whereas the final of the three rounds indicates the attaining of arahantship, this indicates the reviewing knowledge by which the Buddha realized that he had become an arahant, completing his spiritual quest.
sn56.11:12.1: The wheel, like that of the wheel-turning monarch, echoes both the unstoppable conquests of the the ancient Indo-Europeans in their wheeled chariots, and the unstoppable progress of the sun in the sky.
sn56.11:12.2: The cry to the gods is inserted between noting that Koṇḍañña had realized the Dhamma, and the Buddha’s acknowledgement of that fact. This serves to highlight the cosmic significance of Koṇḍañña’s achievement: he showed that others, not just the Buddha, could realize the Dhamma. Some versions of this text lack the passage on the gods, suggesting that it was added later.
sn56.11:13.2: This phrase is only associated with key events in the Buddha’s life (MN 120:17.5). At the conclusion of the Brahmajālasutta the galaxy is more modestly said to tremble (DN 1:3.74.6).
